source_text: Narrantur uisa quaedam, quae huic disputationi non neglegendam uideantur inferre quaestionem. feruntur quippe mortui nonnulli uel in somnis uel alio quocumque modo adparuisse uiuentibus atque ubi eorum corpora iacerent inhumata nescientibus locisque monstratis admonuisse, ut sibi sepultura quae defuerat praeberetur. haec si falsa esse responderimus, contra quorundam scripta fidelium et contra eorum sensus, qui talia sibi accidisse confirmant, inpudenter uenire uidebimur. sed respondendum est non ideo putandum esse mortuos ista sentire, quia haec dicere uel indicare uel petere uidentur in somnis. nam et uiuentes adparent saepe uiuentibus dormientibus, dum se ipsi nesciant adparere, et ab eis haec quae somniauerint audiunt dicentibus, quod eos in somnis uiderint agentes aliquid uel loquentes. si ergo me potest aliquis in somnis uidere sibi aliquid quod factum est indicantem uel etiam quod futurum est praenuntiantem, cum id ego prorsus ignorem et omnino non curem, non solum quid ille somniet, sed utrum dormiente me uigilet, an uigilante me dormiat, an uno eodemque tempore uigilemus ambo siue dormiamus, quando ille somnium uidet, in quo me uidet: quid mirum, si nescientes mortui nec ista sentientes tamen a uiuentibus uidentur in somnis et aliquid dicunt, quod euigilantes uerum esse cognoscant? angelicis igitur operationibus fieri crediderim, siue permittatur desuper siue iubeatur, ut aliquid dicere de sepeliendis corporibus suis uideantur in somnis, cum id penitus nesciant, quorum illa sunt corpora. id autem aliquando utiliter fit siue ad uiuorum qualecumque solacium, ad quos pertinent illi mortui, quorum adparent imagines somniantibus, siue ut his admonitionibus generi humano sepulturae commendetur humanitas, quae, licet defunctis non opituletur, culpanda tamen inreligiositate neglegitur. aliquando autem fallacibus uisis homines in magnos mittuntur errores, quos talia perpeti iustum est. uelut si quisquam uideat in somnis, quod Aeneas uidisse apud inferos poetica falsitate narratur, et ei cuiuspiam non sepulti adpareat imago loquaturque talia, qualia fertur locutus illi fuisse Palinurus, et cum euigilauerit, ibi corpus eius inueniat, ubi iacere inhumatum, cum somniaret, audiuit, admonitus et rogatus, ut sepeliret inuentum, et quia id uerum esse comperit, credat ideo mortuos sepeliri, ut eorum animae ad loca transeant, unde insepultorum animas inferna prohiberi lege somniauit: nonne ita credens plurimum a tramite ueritatis exorbitat?
thought_title: Dream appearances of the dead and burial
orientation: Augustine is answering the objection that the dead must sense their bodies' condition because they sometimes appear in dreams to ask for burial.
pass_a_gloss: Certain visions are reported, which seem to bring a question not to be neglected to this discussion. For some dead people are said to have appeared to the living either in dreams or in some other way, and to have pointed out places to those who did not know where their bodies lay unburied, and to have urged that the burial which had been lacking be provided for them. If we answer that these things are false, we will seem to come shamelessly against the writings of certain faithful people and against the experience of those who affirm that such things happened to them. But it must be answered that the dead are not for that reason to be thought to sense these things, because they seem to say or indicate or ask these things in dreams. For living people also often appear to living people who are sleeping, while they themselves do not know that they appear, and from them those who have dreamed hear these things, saying that they saw them in dreams doing something or speaking. If therefore someone can see me in dreams indicating to him something that has happened or even foretelling something that is to happen, while I myself am completely ignorant of it and do not care at all, not only what he dreams, but whether while I sleep he is awake, or while I am awake he sleeps, or whether we are both awake or both asleep at one and the same time, when he sees a dream in which he sees me: what wonder if the dead, not knowing and not sensing these things, are nevertheless seen by the living in dreams and say something which those who wake up recognize to be true? Therefore I would believe that it happens by angelic operations, whether it is permitted from above or commanded, that they seem to say something in dreams about burying their bodies, while those whose bodies they are know it not at all. And this is sometimes done usefully either for some consolation of the living, to whom those dead belong whose images appear to dreamers, or so that by these admonitions humanity of burial may be commended to the human race, which, although it does not help the dead, is nevertheless neglected with culpable irreligion. But sometimes by deceptive visions people are sent into great errors, which it is just for them to suffer. As if someone should see in dreams what Aeneas is narrated by poetic falsehood to have seen in the underworld, and the image of some unburied person should appear to him and speak such things as Palinurus is said to have spoken to him, and when he wakes up, he should find the body of that person there, where he heard while dreaming that it lay unburied, having been admonished and asked to bury it when found, and because he finds this to be true, he should believe that the dead are buried for this reason, so that their souls may pass to places from which the law of the underworld, as he dreamed, bars the souls of the unburied: does not one believing this go far astray from the path of truth?

choices.why: Glossary term; must use 'burial' and avoid 'interment' or 'sepulture'.
Glossary term for the place of the dead in a poetic or pagan sense; 'hell' is banned.
Renders the likenesses of persons seen in dreams, distinct from the persons themselves; 'apparitions' or 'phantoms' would over-interpret.
Keeps the abstract noun phrase literal; 'humanity' here means the humane practice of burying, not 'humaneness' as a feeling.
Literal rendering of the adverb; 'impudently' is a false friend with a different modern connotation.
Literal rendering; Augustine attributes the dream appearances to the working of angels, not to the dead themselves.

pass_b_english: Certain visions are reported which seem to raise a question that this discussion should not ignore. Some of the dead, it is said, have appeared to the living either in dreams or in some other way, and when the living did not know where their bodies lay unburied, the dead pointed out the places and urged that the burial they had lacked be given to them. If we answer that these reports are false, we will seem to be shamelessly contradicting the writings of some of the faithful and the convictions of those who insist that such things happened to them. But the answer must be that we should not think the dead themselves perceive these things just because they seem to speak or point or ask in dreams. For living people also often appear to living people who are asleep, without knowing that they appear, and the dreamers hear from them the very things they dreamed—that they saw them doing something or speaking. So if someone can see me in a dream telling him something that has happened or even foretelling something that will happen, while I know nothing about it and am not concerned at all—not only what he is dreaming, but whether I am awake while he sleeps, or asleep while he is awake, or whether we are both awake or both asleep at the same time when he has the dream in which he sees me—what wonder is it if the dead, without knowing it and without perceiving these things, are nevertheless seen by the living in dreams and say something that those who wake up recognize as true? I would therefore believe that these things happen through angelic operations, whether permitted from above or commanded, so that the dead seem in dreams to say something about burying their bodies, while those whose bodies they are know nothing of it. And this sometimes happens usefully, either for some comfort to the living to whom those dead belong, whose images appear to dreamers, or so that by these admonitions the humanity of burial may be commended to the human race—which, although it does not help the dead, is still neglected with blameworthy irreligion. Sometimes, however, by deceptive visions people are sent into great errors, which it is just for them to suffer. For example, if someone should see in a dream what Aeneas is said, by poetic falsehood, to have seen in the underworld, and the image of some unburied person should appear to him and speak such words as Palinurus is reported to have spoken to him, and when he wakes up he should find the body in the place where he heard, while dreaming, that it lay unburied—having been admonished and asked to bury what he found—and because he discovers this to be true, he should believe that the dead are buried so that their souls may pass to places from which the souls of the unburied are barred by an underworld law, as he dreamed: would he not, by believing this, go far astray from the path of truth?

problems.why: The participles refer to the dreamer (the living person), not to the body. The dreamer was admonished and asked by the apparition, but the English makes it sound like the body was urged and asked.

problems.quote: the testimony of those who insist that such things happened to them
problems.source_quote: contra eorum sensus, qui talia sibi accidisse confirmant
problems.why: sensus means 'judgment/conviction' here, not 'testimony'; Augustine contrasts writings with the convictions of those affirming such things.
problems.fix: the convictions of those who insist that such things happened to them
problems.ruling: sensus here means 'judgments/convictions' (cf. 'feelings, opinions'), not 'testimony'; Augustine contrasts written accounts with personal convictions, not testimony.

edits.old: urged and asked to bury what he found
edits.new: having been admonished and asked to bury what he found

edits.old: the testimony of those who insist that such things happened to them
edits.new: the convictions of those who insist that such things happened to them

fixed: Changed 'urged and asked' to 'having been admonished and asked' because the Latin participles 'admonitus et rogatus' refer to the dreamer, not the body.
Changed 'testimony' to 'convictions' because 'sensus' here means judgment or conviction, not testimony.

last_rejected.quote: which it is just for them to suffer
last_rejected.why: 'iustum est' means 'it is right/fitting' (divinely appropriate), not 'just' in sense of deserved punishment.
last_rejected.fix: which it is right that they should suffer
last_rejected.ruling: 'iustum est' covers both 'just' and 'fitting'; 'just for them to suffer' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: the image of some unburied person should appear to him
last_rejected.source_quote: ei cuiuspiam non sepulti adpareat imago
last_rejected.why: Latin 'cuiuspiam' = 'of someone/anyone'; English 'some' loses the indefiniteness, but more critically, 'unburied person' should be 'of someone not buried' to match genitive.
last_rejected.fix: the image of someone not buried should appear to him
last_rejected.ruling: 'some unburied person' adequately renders 'cuiuspiam non sepulti'; indefiniteness is preserved by 'some'.

last_rejected.why: 'cum somniaret' = 'while he was dreaming' (temporal); 'as he dreamed' could mean 'because/according as', changing the causal logic.
last_rejected.ruling: 'as he dreamed' naturally reads temporally here; no real ambiguity or meaning change from 'cum somniaret'.
